Jump to:ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWYZ


Definitions of key terms used throughout the book.






Term
Definition




adjusted \(R^2\)
A version of \(R^2\) that penalizes a model for adding predictors that do not improve fit, so it can decrease when useless variables are added; preferred for comparing multiple regression models.


adjusted deviance \(R^2\)
A version of deviance \(R^2\) that penalizes the model for adding predictors, so it can decrease when useless variables are added.


adjusted means
Group averages recalculated by an ANCOVA as if every participant had started at the same covariate value; also called estimated marginal means.


algorithmic accountability
The obligation to hold algorithms and their creators responsible for the outcomes the algorithms produce, including biased or harmful decisions.


algorithmic bias
Systematic unfairness produced when an algorithm learns from biased historical data and applies that pattern at scale.


alternative hypothesis
The claim that an effect, a difference, or a relationship exists in the population, written \(H_1\); this is the position the researcher is actually trying to prove, and it is accepted only when the data provide strong enough evidence.


analytic integrity
The obligation to analyze data honestly, deciding what to test before looking at the data and reporting all results, including null findings.


ANCOVA
Analysis of Covariance: a hybrid of ANOVA and regression that compares group means while adjusting for one or more continuous covariates.


anonymity
A privacy condition in which no one, not even the researcher, can link data back to the individual.


ANOVA
Analysis of Variance: a statistical test that compares the means of three or more independent groups to determine whether at least one pair differs significantly; the natural extension of the independent sample t-test.


area under the curve (AUC)
A summary of a model’s classification performance, equal to the probability that the model ranks a randomly chosen positive case above a randomly chosen negative case; 0.5 is chance and 1.0 is perfect.


ARIMA
AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average: a forecasting model that combines recent momentum, removal of trend, and correction for past shocks to project future values.


association
A systematic connection between two categorical variables, meaning knowing the category of one gives information about the other; the opposite of independence.


association metric
A standardized measure of the strength of a relationship between categorical variables, the categorical equivalent of an effect size; Phi and Cramér’s V are the two primary examples.


autocorrelation
The correlation of a variable with its own past values, meaning observations that are close in time tend to be related.


automated model selection
A software procedure that adds or removes predictors automatically based on statistical criteria; useful for screening, but it can override theoretical judgment and should not be used on autopilot.


autoregressive (AR)
The ARIMA component that uses a series’ own recent values, or momentum, to help predict the next value.


bar plot
A graph that displays the frequency or proportion of observations in each category using rectangular bars, with gaps between bars to signal categorical data.


base-10 logarithm
A logarithm using base 10, written log10; it compresses large values and is often used to linearize exponential growth.


baseline group
The category of a categorical predictor that is left out of the indicator variables and absorbed into the intercept; every other category is interpreted relative to it (also called the reference group).


between-groups variation
The part of total variation that measures how far the group averages are from one another; in ANOVA it represents the signal, or the effect of the factor.


between-subjects design
A design in which different participants are assigned to different groups, so comparisons are made between separate people.


bias
A systematic error that pushes results away from the truth in a particular direction; unlike random variability, bias does not disappear with larger sample sizes.


bimodal
A distribution with two distinct peaks, often signaling that two different groups are mixed together in the data.


bin
An interval used in a histogram to group values of a numerical variable; each bar represents one bin and its height shows how many observations fall within that range.


binary outcome
An outcome with exactly two possible categories, such as survived or died.


blocking
Converting a known nuisance variable into categorical groups (blocks) so its variation is removed from the error term, improving the comparison.


Bonferroni correction
A conservative post hoc method that lowers the threshold for each comparison to control the family-wise error rate; it strongly protects against Type I errors but raises the risk of Type II errors.


box plot
A graph that summarizes the distribution of a numerical variable using five key values (minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum), with individual points flagging potential outliers; useful for comparing distributions across categories.


bubble plot
A scatterplot extended to three numerical variables: two define point positions on the axes, and a third determines the size of each bubble.


case-control study
An observational design that selects people who already have an outcome (cases) and people who do not (controls), then looks back at past exposures; also called a retrospective design.


categorical variable
A variable that places each observation into a group or category; values are labels rather than quantities and do not support arithmetic operations.


ceiling effect
Occurs when many observations pile up at the maximum possible value, preventing detection of further differences among high performers.


cell
A specific subgroup created by crossing the levels of two or more factors in a factorial design.


censored data
Data in which you know a value exists beyond a certain threshold but do not know its exact amount (e.g., recorded as “40+”).


central limit theorem
The theorem that the distribution of sample means approaches a predictable bell curve as sample size grows, regardless of the shape of the original data; this is what allows t-tests to work with skewed data when the sample is large enough.


chi-square goodness-of-fit test
A test that compares the distribution of one categorical variable in a sample against an external baseline distribution, such as a census profile.


chi-square statistic
The test statistic for chi-square tests, formed by summing the squared gaps between observed and expected counts, each divided by the expected count; larger values mean the data deviate more from the null expectation.


chi-square test for homogeneity
A test that compares the distribution of one categorical variable across two or more separate populations to see whether the proportions are the same.


chi-square test for independence
A test that asks whether two categorical variables measured in a single sample are associated, using a cross-tabulation of their counts.


coefficient of determination
The proportion of variability in one variable that is explained by another, written \(R^2\) and calculated by squaring the correlation \(r\); often reported as a percentage.


Cohen’s \(d\)
A standardized effect size that divides the difference between two means by the standard deviation, expressing the gap in standard-deviation units so results can be compared across studies.


communality
The proportion of a variable’s variation that is shared with other variables because they measure the same underlying factor.


component
A summary variable produced by PCA, which compresses all variance, including unique variance and measurement error, into a smaller set of dimensions.


confidence interval
A range of plausible values for a true population mean or difference, built from sample data; a 95% confidence interval (CI) comes from a procedure that captures the true value in about 95% of repeated samples.


confidentiality
A privacy condition in which the researcher can link data to participants but promises to keep their identities secret.


confirmatory factor analysis (CFA)
A factor analysis used when the researcher already has a theory and specifies in advance how many factors exist and which variables belong to each, then tests how well that model fits.


confounding factor
A third variable that influences both the predictor and the response variable, distorting the apparent relationship; also called a confounding variable.


confounding variable
A hidden or unmeasured factor that is linked to both the groups you are comparing and the outcome, so it can make two variables appear connected even when one does not cause the other.


confusion matrix
A 2 by 2 table that compares a prediction rule’s yes/no calls with the actual outcomes, showing true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives.


continuous variable
A numerical variable that can take any value within a range, limited only by measurement precision (e.g., height, weight, time).


control
The practice of holding outside variables constant in an experiment so they do not interfere with the results.


control for
To mathematically hold a variable constant in a model so that the unique effect of another predictor can be isolated.


control group
The group in an experiment that does not receive the treatment being tested, used as a baseline for comparison with the treatment group.


Cook’s Distance
A measure of how much a regression model changes when one data point is removed (also called Cook’s D); values above 1.0 are generally treated as highly influential.


correlation matrix
A table showing the correlation coefficient between every pair of variables in a set.


covariate
A continuous background variable included in a model to adjust for its effect, such as a baseline score.


Cramér’s V
An association metric for categorical variables used when the cross-tabulation is larger than 2 by 2, ranging from 0 (no association) to 1 (perfect association).


Cronbach’s alpha
A statistic (written \(\alpha\)) that measures the internal consistency of a survey, ranging from 0 to 1; values of 0.70 or higher are generally considered acceptable in social science research.


cross-tabulation
A table that counts observations in each combination of categories for two categorical variables; also called a contingency table.


cyclical patterns
Predictable, repeating fluctuations in a time series that occur at regular intervals; in social science this is often called seasonality.


data governance
The overarching rules, policies, and standards that determine how data are collected, stored, and used.


data reduction
The goal of summarizing many observed variables with a smaller number of components or factors, without necessarily uncovering hidden constructs.


data stewardship
The day-to-day ethical responsibility of the individual researcher to protect and handle data properly.


data transformation
A mathematical change to a variable, such as a log transformation, applied to make its distribution better meet a model’s assumptions.


data triage
The initial pass through a dataset to decide what to keep, drop, or treat as missing before formal analysis.


degrees of freedom
A number tied to sample size that the t-distribution uses when producing a p-value; for a single sample t-test it equals \(n - 1\) and is reported in parentheses after \(t\) in APA style.


de-identification
Removing or masking identifying details from a dataset while keeping a separate key that can link records back to individuals; not the same as anonymity.


descriptive statistics
Numerical summaries that describe a dataset, such as the mean, median, standard deviation, and proportion.


deviance
A measure of badness of fit in logistic regression, analogous to residual error; lower values mean predictions are closer to the observed outcomes.


deviance \(R^2\)
A pseudo-\(R^2\) for logistic regression that measures how much the model reduces deviance compared with a model with no predictors.


discrete variable
A numerical variable that takes on distinct, separate values, typically counts (e.g., number of siblings).


distribution
The pattern of how values of a variable are spread across its range; described by center, spread, shape, and unusual observations.


Dunnett’s test
A post hoc test that compares several groups against one designated baseline group, saving power by skipping comparisons among the other groups.


effect size
A standardized number describing how large a difference or relationship is, independent of sample size, used to judge whether a statistically significant result is large enough to matter.


epsilon-squared (\(\varepsilon^2\))
An effect size for the Kruskal-Wallis Test: the share of the variation in the ranks that the groups account for, read like \(R^2\).


equal variance (homoscedasticity)
The assumption that the vertical spread of residuals stays roughly constant across the range of the predictor variable; a fan or cone shape signals heteroscedasticity.


ethics of omission
The ethical responsibility attached to decisions about which data to keep, drop, or treat as missing, because those choices determine whose experiences count.


expected count
The count a chi-square test would expect in a cell if the null hypothesis were true; every expected count should be at least 5 for the standard test to be trustworthy.


experiment
A study in which researchers deliberately manipulate one or more variables to observe the direct effect on an outcome, using control and randomization to support a cause-and-effect conclusion.


exploratory factor analysis (EFA)
A factor analysis used when the researcher does not know the underlying structure and lets the correlations reveal how many factors exist and which variables belong together.


extrapolation
Using a regression model to predict outside the range of predictor values observed in the data, which is risky because the relationship may change.


factor
The categorical variable that divides a sample into the groups being compared; also called the treatment variable.


factor analysis
A statistical method that explains correlations among observed variables by positing one or more hidden factors, separating shared communality from unique variance.


factorial design
A study design that crosses two or more categorical factors so that every combination of levels is represented, allowing main effects and interactions to be estimated.


factor level
One of the specific categories that make up a factor; also called a treatment level.


factor loading
A weight between -1 and 1 that measures the strength and direction of the relationship between an observed variable and a factor; loadings of about 0.40 or higher are usually treated as meaningful.


factor matrix
A table showing each observed variable’s loadings on each extracted factor, often after rotation, along with communality and uniqueness.


false negative
A missed case: the prediction rule says no when the event happened.


false positive
A false alarm: the prediction rule says yes when the event did not happen.


family-wise error rate
The overall probability of making at least one Type I error across a family of comparisons; post hoc tests are designed to control it.


Fisher’s Exact Test
A test for categorical associations designed for small samples, used when an expected count falls below 5.


floor effect
Occurs when many observations cluster at the minimum possible value, compressing the range of observable variation.


forecasting
Predicting future values of a time series from its historical patterns.


F-statistic
The ANOVA test statistic, calculated as the ratio of between-groups variation (signal) to within-groups variation (noise); its meaning depends on the degrees of freedom, so it is interpreted through its p-value.


Glass’s delta
An effect size that divides the difference between two group means by the control group’s standard deviation, used when the two groups have different spreads.


global ANOVA
The overall ANOVA F-test that asks whether any group means differ, before post hoc tests identify which specific pairs differ.


grouping variable
A categorical variable used to divide observations into groups within a plot, often shown through different colors or shapes, so patterns can be compared across categories.


halo effect
A cognitive bias in which a strong positive impression in one area leads a person to rate a target favorably across unrelated categories, producing a uniform blur of correlations.


Hedges’ \(g\)
A version of Cohen’s \(d\) with a small-sample correction, typically used when the total sample is under about 20 people and interpreted the same way as \(d\).


histogram
A graph for a single numerical variable that groups values into adjacent bins with no gaps between bars; bar heights show how many observations fall in each bin.


homogeneity of regression slopes
The ANCOVA assumption that the relationship between the covariate and the response is parallel across groups, checked by testing the covariate-by-group interaction.


Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test
A test of whether a logistic model’s predicted probabilities fit the observed outcomes; unlike most tests, a large p-value is the desired result because the null hypothesis says the model fits well.


human subjects
People who participate in research and whose data or biological material are collected and analyzed.


hypothesis testing
A formal procedure for deciding whether an observed effect is real or could plausibly be explained by random variation, by weighing the data against a null hypothesis.


imputation
Replacing a missing value with a statistically estimated value so that the observation can be kept in the analysis.


independence
In study design, the assumption that observations do not influence one another; in categorical data, the property that knowing one variable’s category gives no information about another (the opposite of association).


independent sample t-test
A t-test that compares the means of two separate, unrelated groups to see whether their difference is statistically significant.


indicator variable
A numerical variable coded 1 or 0 to represent whether an observation belongs to a category, allowing categorical predictors to enter a regression equation; also called a dummy variable.


influential point
A data point whose removal would noticeably change a model’s slope or intercept, usually because it combines high leverage with a large residual.


institutional review board (IRB)
An independent committee that evaluates research protocols before a study begins to protect human subjects, keep risk minimal, and safeguard vulnerable populations.


integrated (I)
The ARIMA component that temporarily removes the long-term trend, usually by differencing, so cyclical patterns can be analyzed on a stable baseline.


interaction
A situation in which the effect of one predictor on the response variable changes depending on the value of another predictor.


interaction effect
The result of an interaction: the effect of one factor depends on the level of another, so its size or direction changes across groups.


interaction plot
A graph of group means with one line per level of a second factor; parallel lines suggest no interaction, while converging, diverging, or crossing lines suggest one.


internal consistency
How well the different items on a survey hang together, which a researcher must establish before adding the items into a single overall score.


interquartile range (IQR)
The spread of the middle 50 percent of data, calculated as Q3 minus Q1; resistant to outliers and paired naturally with the median for skewed distributions.


irregular movements
Random noise, sudden shocks, or anomalies in a time series that do not repeat.


jitter plot
A graph that randomly nudges points sideways so overlapping observations stay visible; used to compare the vertical spread of groups when checking equal variances.


Kruskal-Wallis Test
A nonparametric test that compares three or more independent groups by ranking all observations; the rank-based alternative to a one-way ANOVA.


lag
The number of time periods by which a series is shifted to compare a value with an earlier value; a lag-1 comparison pairs each week with the week before.


latent construct
A hidden concept, such as social appeal or socioeconomic status, that is not measured directly but is inferred from several observed variables.


law of diminishing returns
The pattern in which each additional unit of a predictor produces a smaller improvement in the outcome, creating a curve that rises sharply and then flattens.


left-skewed
A distribution whose longer tail extends toward lower values; also called negatively skewed.


Levene’s test
A formal hypothesis test for equal group variances; this book recommends visual checks and the 2X rule instead, because using a test to gatekeep another test compounds error.


leverage
The potential a data point has to pull a regression line toward itself, which is greatest when its predictor value sits at the extreme edge of the observed range.


Likert scale
An ordinal survey scale, such as disagree, neutral, agree, whose categories have a clear order but unknown distances between them.


linear correlation
A number \(r\) between -1 and 1 that measures the direction and strength of a straight-line relationship between two numerical variables; the sign gives the direction and the distance from zero gives the strength.


linearity
The assumption that the true relationship between two numerical variables is a straight line, checked by looking for curves in a residual plot.


linearize
To transform data mathematically so that a curved relationship becomes approximately straight, allowing a linear regression model to be used.


linear trend
The straight-line relationship between calendar time and a variable, describing its long-term trajectory rather than short-term momentum.


listwise deletion
Dropping every observation that has a missing value on any variable in the analysis.


logarithmic transformation
A transformation that takes the logarithm of a variable, compressing large values and stretching small ones; often used to linearize an exponential or diminishing-returns relationship.


logistic regression
A regression model for a binary outcome that estimates how predictors affect the odds of the outcome; the odds ratio is its basic building block.


logit
Another name for the log-odds, and the quantity a logistic regression model estimates directly.


log-odds
The natural logarithm of the odds of an outcome; a scale centered at zero that can be modeled with a straight line.


longitudinal data
Data collected from the same participants at multiple time points; the repeated observations are dependent, so a standard one-way ANOVA does not apply.


main effects
The individual predictors that make up an interaction term; when an interaction is included in a model, the main effects must also be included.


Mann-Whitney U Test
A nonparametric test that compares two independent groups by pooling and ranking all observations; requires the two distributions to have roughly the same shape.


margin of error
The width of a confidence interval around an estimate; a smaller margin of error means a more precise estimate, and increasing the sample size shrinks it.


matched pair t-test
A t-test for data in which each observation in one group is linked to a specific observation in another, such as the same person measured before and after an intervention; it tests whether the average within-pair difference is zero.


maximum likelihood (ML)
A factor extraction method that assumes multivariate normality and allows formal fit tests and confidence intervals; it can distort loadings when that assumption fails.


McNemar’s test
A test for paired categorical data that compares two dependent proportions by focusing on the pairs where the two responses disagree.


mean
The average: add all values together and divide by the number of observations; uses every value, making it informative but sensitive to extreme values.


measurement error
Random noise in a measurement caused by imperfect measurement conditions, not by the construct being measured; it is part of unique variance.


measures of center
Numerical summaries that describe a typical or central value in a distribution, such as the mean, median, and mode; the type of data determines which measure is appropriate.


measures of spread
Numerical summaries that describe how spread out or variable the observations are, such as the range, interquartile range, and standard deviation.


median
The middle value when all observations are ordered from smallest to largest; half the data fall above it and half below, and it is resistant to outliers and skew.


median difference
The median of the within-pair differences in paired data, used as the center that the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test evaluates.


meta-analysis
A technique that mathematically combines the results of many independent studies on the same topic, pooling their data to build a stronger argument than any single study can.


minimal risk
The standard that the probability and magnitude of harm in a study are no greater than those encountered in ordinary daily life or routine tests.


missing at random (MAR)
Missingness that depends on other observed variables in the dataset, rather than being purely random or systematically tied to the missing value itself.


missing completely at random (MCAR)
Missingness that occurs with equal probability for all observations, unrelated to any variable, observed or unobserved.


missing not at random (MNAR)
Missingness that is systematically related to the missing value itself (e.g., low-income students less likely to report income), introducing bias that is difficult to correct.


modal
Refers to the number of prominent peaks in a distribution: unimodal (one peak), bimodal (two peaks), or multimodal (three or more peaks).


mode
The most frequently occurring value in a dataset; the only measure of center appropriate for nominal data.


model diagnostics
The checks researchers run to verify a model’s assumptions, such as independence, mutually exclusive factor levels, normal residuals, and equal variances.


monotonic
A relationship that consistently moves in one direction, either upward or downward, though it may curve; it cannot reverse direction.


Mood’s Median test
A nonparametric alternative to ANOVA used when group variances are unequal.


mosaic plot
A graph that displays the relationship between two categorical variables using rectangles whose areas correspond to the proportions of observations in each combination of categories.


moving average (MA)
The ARIMA component that adjusts forecasts for recent random shocks or irregular movements.


multicollinearity
Heavy overlap among predictors that makes it hard for a model to tell which variable is driving the change, producing unstable and unreliable slopes.


multimodal
A distribution with three or more distinct peaks.


multiple comparisons
Testing several hypotheses on the same data without adjusting the significance level, which inflates the family-wise error rate.


multiple logistic regression
A logistic regression model that predicts a binary outcome using two or more predictors at once.


multiple regression
A statistical method that predicts a single continuous response variable using two or more predictors at the same time.


mutually exclusive
A requirement that each observation belongs to exactly one level of a factor, with no overlap between groups.


noise
Random variation among individuals that is unrelated to the factor being studied; in ANOVA it is the within-groups variation.


nominal variable
A categorical variable whose categories have no natural order (e.g., eye color, country of birth).


nonparametric tests
Tests that do not require a normal distribution, typically by analyzing ranks instead of raw values; used for small samples, skewed data, or ordinal outcomes.


non-resistant measure
A statistical measure that shifts noticeably when extreme values or outliers are present; the mean is an example.


non-response bias
A type of bias that occurs when the people who choose not to complete a survey are different from those who do, so the collected data do not represent the full group.


normal curve
The symmetric, bell-shaped curve that describes a normal distribution, with most observations clustered near the center and becoming rarer toward the tails; also called the bell curve.


normal distribution
A specific symmetric, unimodal “bell curve” shape common in nature and measurement data; about 68% of observations fall within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three.


normality
In regression, the assumption that the residuals form a roughly bell-shaped distribution; the raw predictor and response variables do not need to be normal.


normality test
A formal hypothesis test, such as Anderson-Darling or Shapiro-Wilk, that checks whether residuals are normally distributed; a low p-value suggests non-normality, but this book uses them only as a tiebreaker.


nuisance variable
A background variable that affects the outcome but is not the main focus of the study; left uncontrolled, it adds noise to the comparison.


null hypothesis
The default assumption of no effect, no difference, or no relationship, written \(H_0\); it always uses exact equality (\(=\)) and stands unless the data provide strong evidence against it.


numerical variable
A variable that takes on values representing quantities and supports arithmetic operations (e.g., GPA, age, hours studied).


observational study
A study in which researchers observe individuals and measure variables of interest without manipulating the environment, recording the world as it naturally exists.


observed variable
A variable that is directly measured, such as a survey item, and used as an indicator of a latent construct.


odds
The probability of an event divided by the probability of the event not happening; odds of 4 mean four events for every one non-event.


odds ratio
The odds of an outcome in one group divided by the odds of the same outcome in a baseline group; the standard measure of risk in case-control studies.


omitted variable bias
Bias that occurs when a confounding variable is left out of a model, so the included predictor’s slope absorbs the missing variable’s effect and becomes inaccurate.


one-sided test
A hypothesis test that looks for an effect in only one direction; choosing it after seeing the data or without justification halves the p-value and is a form of p-hacking.


operationalization
The process of defining exactly how you will measure an abstract concept in your study, bridging a theoretical idea and the concrete data you will eventually analyze.


ordinal
A categorical variable whose categories have a meaningful order but unknown distances between adjacent categories.


ordinal logistic regression
A regression model for an ordinal outcome with three or more ranked categories.


ordinal variable
A categorical variable whose categories follow a meaningful ranking (e.g., education level, satisfaction rating), though distances between adjacent categories are not necessarily equal.


outlier
A data point that strays far from the pattern set by the rest of the data, often producing a large residual in a regression model.


overfitting
A modeling failure in which a model becomes so complex that it memorizes random noise in the sample instead of the true underlying pattern.


paired data
Observations that come in linked pairs, such as two people in the same interaction or the same person measured twice; standard chi-square tests assume independent observations, so paired categorical data require McNemar’s test.


parameter
A numerical summary that describes an entire population; usually fixed but unknown, estimated from sample statistics.


Pareto chart
A bar plot for categorical data with bars sorted from most to least frequent, often combining rare categories into a single “Other” bar so the largest categories stand out.


parsimony
The principle that the simplest model that explains the data well is preferred, avoiding unnecessary complexity.


partitioning variation
The ANOVA process of splitting total variation into between-groups variation (signal) and within-groups variation (noise).


percentile
The percentage of observations that fall below a given value; for example, scoring at the 90th percentile means you scored higher than 90% of the comparison group.


p-hacking
Running many tests or model variations on the same data until a p-value below .05 appears, which inflates the Type I error rate and is an ethical violation.


Phi (\(\phi\))
An association metric for a 2 by 2 cross-tabulation, ranging from 0 (no association) to 1 (perfect association).


point estimate
A single predicted value produced by plugging a specific predictor value into a regression equation; in regression it estimates the mean response for all observations with that predictor value.


population
The entire group of individuals or observations you want to draw conclusions about.


post hoc test
A follow-up comparison run after a significant ANOVA to identify which specific groups differ while controlling the family-wise error rate; also called post hoc analysis.


power analysis
The process of calculating, before a study begins, the sample size needed to detect an effect of a given size with a chosen level of statistical power.


power curves
A graph showing how statistical power rises as sample size increases, with separate curves for different effect sizes.


practical significance
Whether an effect is large enough to matter in practice, judged from an effect size or confidence interval rather than from a p-value alone.


predicted probability
The model’s estimated probability that a specific observation has the outcome, produced by converting the logit back to a 0-to-1 scale.


prediction interval
A range that is likely to contain the response value for a single new observation at a given predictor value; it is wider than a confidence interval for the mean because individuals vary more than averages.


predictor variable
A variable used to predict or explain the response variable in a regression model; also called an independent variable.


principal axis factoring (PAF)
A factor extraction method that makes few distributional assumptions and is the usual choice for ordinal survey data in exploratory factor analysis.


principal components analysis (PCA)
A data reduction method that compresses all variance, including unique variance and measurement error, into components; it does not separate shared communality from noise.


proportion
The fraction of observations falling into a given category; commonly reported for two-category categorical variables (e.g., 80 out of 200 = 0.40 or 40%).


proportion of variance
The share of total variance explained by a factor or component, used to judge how much each one contributes.


protocol
A detailed plan submitted to an Institutional Review Board that describes the research question, participants, consent process, and data protection; approval is required before data collection begins.


proxy variable
A measurable characteristic that stands in for an unobservable or difficult-to-measure concept.


p-value
The probability of seeing data at least as surprising as yours if the null hypothesis were true; a small p-value means the data would be unusual under \(H_0\) and counts as evidence against it.


Q-Q plot
A plot that compares observed residuals with the values expected under a normal distribution; points that hug the diagonal line support normality, and it is treated as equivalent to a normal probability plot.


quartile
Values that divide a dataset into four equal parts: Q1 (25th percentile), Q2 (the median, 50th percentile), and Q3 (75th percentile).


randomization
The random assignment of subjects or treatments in an experiment so that unavoidable natural differences are spread evenly across groups, keeping hidden biases from skewing the results.


rare events rule
The guideline that a logistic regression needs roughly 10 to 15 occurrences of the least common outcome for each predictor, so rare outcomes require larger samples.


receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve
A plot of sensitivity against the false positive rate across all possible decision thresholds, used to compare classification models.


relative risk
The probability of an outcome in one group divided by the probability of the same outcome in a baseline group; intuitive for cohort studies but not valid for case-control designs.


reliability
The consistency of a measurement: a reliable tool gives you the same result every time you measure the same phenomenon under the same conditions.


reliable estimator
An estimator whose values cluster close to the true parameter across repeated samples.


repeated measures ANOVA
An ANOVA for a within-subjects design in which the same participants are measured at multiple time points or conditions, so each person serves as their own baseline.


replication
Conducting an experiment on a large enough number of subjects so that the results are not just a statistical fluke.


research goal
A general statement about the phenomenon you want to understand; broad and directional, but usually too abstract to test directly.


research question
A specific, measurable relationship between defined variables that you can observe and record, narrowed down from a broad research goal.


residual
The difference between an observed value and the value predicted by a model, so a positive residual means the model underpredicted and a negative residual means it overpredicted.


residual plot
A graph with the predictor variable on the horizontal axis and the residuals on the vertical axis, used to check for curves, unequal spread, and structural patterns that a straight-line model would miss.


resistant measure
A statistical measure not strongly influenced by extreme values or outliers; the median is an example.


response variable
The variable a regression model is trying to predict, traditionally plotted on the vertical axis; it must be a true numerical measurement.


right-skewed
A distribution whose longer tail extends toward higher values; also called positively skewed.


Rosenthal’s \(r\)
An effect size for the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank and Mann-Whitney U tests: the absolute \(z\)-value divided by the square root of the sample size, read with the same guidelines as a correlation.


rotation
A mathematical adjustment of factor axes that maximizes high loadings and minimizes low ones, producing a clearer simple structure without changing the underlying communality.


sample
A subset of a population, the portion from which you collect data.


sample size
The number of observations in a sample, usually written \(n\); larger samples reduce random error and increase statistical power.


scatterplot
A graph that displays the relationship between two numerical variables by placing each observation as a point; used to assess direction, form, and strength of the relationship.


scree chart
A line graph of the variance explained by each successive factor, used to choose how many factors to keep by locating the elbow where the curve flattens.


segmented bar chart
A chart that compares two categorical variables by giving each group a bar of equal height (100%) divided into segments showing the proportion in each category of the second variable; also called a 100% stacked bar chart.


selective group analysis
Testing many subgroups and reporting only the significant ones, a form of p-hacking that hides the failed tests.


sensitivity
The true positive rate: the percentage of actual events that a prediction rule correctly catches.


signal
The portion of variation that reflects the real effect being studied, such as differences between group means; in ANOVA it is the between-groups variation.


significance level
The threshold of evidence, written \(\alpha\) and usually set at .05, that a researcher requires before rejecting the null hypothesis.


significance stars
Symbols such as *, **, and *** placed next to coefficients in journal tables to mark p-values below common thresholds (.05, .01, and .001).


Sign Test
A flexible nonparametric test for paired data that compares the direction of within-pair differences; used when the Wilcoxon symmetry assumption fails.


simple structure
A clean factor pattern in which each observed variable loads strongly on one factor and weakly on the others.


single sample t-test
A t-test that compares the mean of one sample against a known, fixed benchmark, such as a national average or a clinical cutoff.


skewness
The extent to which a distribution is asymmetric, with a longer tail extending toward one side; right-skewed distributions trail toward high values and left-skewed distributions toward low values.


slope
The rate of change in a regression model: the predicted change in the response variable for each one-unit increase in the predictor variable.


Spearman’s Rho
A nonparametric correlation that ranks both variables before correlating them, measuring the strength of a monotonic relationship; also used for ordinal data.


specificity
The true negative rate: the percentage of actual non-events that a prediction rule correctly ignores.


specific variance
Variation that is real and systematic but unique to a single observed variable, not shared with other variables; part of unique variance.


standard deviation
A measure of how much individual values typically deviate from the mean; small values indicate tight clustering, large values indicate wide scattering.


standard error
The typical amount by which a sample statistic is expected to vary from sample to sample because of random chance; it is the denominator of the t-statistic.


standardized residual
A cell’s contribution to a chi-square test, scaled so that values beyond about plus or minus 2 indicate a significant over- or under-representation.


statistic
A numerical summary calculated from sample data; varies from sample to sample because different samples contain different individuals.


statistically significant
A result is statistically significant when its p-value is below the chosen significance level, meaning the data provide enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis.


statistical power
The probability that a study will detect a true effect if one exists; it is the complement of a Type II error, and researchers generally aim for at least 80%.


statistical question
A formal question that (1) requires gathering data, (2) accounts for natural variability from sample to sample, and (3) names the specific statistical measure you will use to compare groups.


summated scale
A measurement tool that asks several different, targeted questions about the same concept and then combines the responses into a single overall score.


symmetric
A distribution whose left half mirrors its right half; if folded at the center, both sides would line up closely.


three-way ANOVA
An ANOVA that tests three categorical factors at once, producing three main effects, three two-way interactions, and one three-way interaction; powerful but hard to interpret.


time series analysis
The analysis of data collected in chronological order, breaking it into trend, cyclical patterns, and irregular movements so the series can be understood and forecast.


time series plot
A line chart with time on the horizontal axis and the measured variable on the vertical axis, preserving the chronological order of the data.


total variation
The overall spread among all observations in a dataset before it is split into between-groups and within-groups parts.


transparency
The practice of openly publishing methods, models, and analytical steps so outside experts can audit and reproduce the work.


treatment
The specific condition or category that distinguishes the groups being compared, whether researchers assign it or it occurs naturally.


treatment group
The subset of participants who fall into one particular level of a factor.


trend
The long-term, overarching direction of a time series, meaning whether its baseline is generally rising, falling, or stable.


true negative
A correct rejection: the prediction rule says no and the event did not happen.


true positive
A hit: the prediction rule says yes and the event happened.


truncated data
Data in which observations beyond a certain threshold are excluded entirely and never appear in the dataset (e.g., only enrolling students who scored above 70).


t-statistic
A signal-to-noise ratio calculated by dividing the gap between a sample result and the hypothesized value by the standard error; software converts it into a p-value.


t-test
A family of hypothesis tests for comparing means, including the single sample, matched pair, and independent sample versions.


Tukey’s HSD
A post hoc test that compares every pair of group means while controlling the family-wise error rate; the standard choice when all pairwise comparisons matter.


t-value
A predictor’s slope divided by its standard error, used as a rough measure of signal strength; another name for the t-statistic.


two-way ANOVA
An ANOVA that tests the effects of two categorical factors at once, including their main effects and interaction.


Type I error
A false alarm (a false positive): rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true; the significance level sets the rate at which this error occurs.


Type II error
A missed signal (a false negative): failing to reject the null hypothesis when a real effect exists, often because the study lacked enough evidence or statistical power to detect it.


unimodal
A distribution with one clear peak; the most common shape encountered in practice.


unique variance
The proportion of a variable’s variation that is not shared with other variables, made up of specific variance and measurement error; also called uniqueness.


validity
Whether a measurement actually captures what you claim it is measuring; a measure can be reliable (consistent) yet still invalid if it is not measuring the intended concept.


variance
A measure of spread equal to the average squared deviation from the mean; ANOVA partitions this variability into between-groups and within-groups parts.


variance inflation factor (VIF)
A diagnostic for multicollinearity that measures how much a predictor’s variance is inflated by its overlap with other predictors; values above 5 signal dangerous overlap.


vulnerable populations
Groups whose ability to give free and informed consent may be compromised, such as prisoners, children, or students under institutional pressure.


Welch’s t-test
A version of the independent sample t-test that adjusts the degrees of freedom when the two groups have unequal variances, producing a more trustworthy p-value.


Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
A nonparametric test for paired data that compares the median difference by ranking the within-pair differences; requires the differences to be roughly symmetric.


within-groups variation
The part of total variation that measures the random differences among individuals inside the same group; in ANOVA it represents the noise.


within-subjects design
A design in which the same participants are measured under multiple conditions or time points, so comparisons are made within each person.


y-intercept
The predicted value of the response variable when the predictor variable equals zero; it anchors the regression line as a baseline.


zero-inflated
A distribution with a large pile of zeros and a small number of high values, so the mean is pulled away from the typical observation.

B.1 acs_2023.csv
Every dataset used in this book is available as a CSV file, with one row per observation and one column per variable. Each section below names the file, describes it, lists its variables in a table, explains how the data were collected, and cites the source. Data files as of November 4, 2026.
Download any file from its section, or get all 22 files and this key together as one ZIP archive.
Description. This dataset contains demographic, economic, and lifestyle information from a sample of individuals living in the United States, drawn from the 2023 American Community Survey.
File. A comma-separated values (.csv) file containing 10,000 observations (rows) and 9 variables (columns).
Download acs_2023.csv (CSV file, 248 KB)
Details. The American Community Survey (ACS) is an ongoing demographics survey administered by the United States Census Bureau. It is distributed annually to a random sample of approximately 3.5 million households, representing about 3% of all U.S. households. The Census Bureau eventually makes a heavily anonymized 1% random sample of all U.S. residents available to the public. To create this specific dataset, a random sub-sample of \(n = 10,000\) individuals was drawn directly from the publicly available 2023 ACS data.
Source. United States Census Bureau. (2023). American Community Survey. https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs

B.2 amas_math_anxiety.csv
Description. This dataset contains individual item-level responses measuring mathematics anxiety using the 9-item Abbreviated Mathematics Anxiety Scale (AMAS). The subjects are a large sample of adult workers evaluating their subjective tension and anxiety across various academic and testing scenarios.
File. A comma-separated values (.csv) file containing 2,200 observations (rows) and 9 variables (columns).
Download amas_math_anxiety.csv (CSV file, 39 KB)

Variables in amas_math_anxiety.csv, with data type and coding key.







Variable Name
Data Type
Description and Coding Keys




item_1
Numerical
Subjective anxiety rating when having to use the tables in the back of a math book, recorded on a \(1 \text{ to } 5\) scale where a value of \(1\) indicates low anxiety and \(5\) indicates high anxiety.


item_2
Numerical
Subjective anxiety rating when thinking about an upcoming math test one day before, recorded on a \(1 \text{ to } 5\) scale where a value of \(1\) indicates low anxiety and \(5\) indicates high anxiety.


item_3
Numerical
Subjective anxiety rating when watching a teacher work an algebraic equation on the blackboard, recorded on a \(1 \text{ to } 5\) scale where a value of \(1\) indicates low anxiety and \(5\) indicates high anxiety.


item_4
Numerical
Subjective anxiety rating when taking an examination in a math course, recorded on a \(1 \text{ to } 5\) scale where a value of \(1\) indicates low anxiety and \(5\) indicates high anxiety.


item_5
Numerical
Subjective anxiety rating when being given a homework assignment of many difficult problems due the next class meeting, recorded on a \(1 \text{ to } 5\) scale where a value of \(1\) indicates low anxiety and \(5\) indicates high anxiety.


item_6
Numerical
Subjective anxiety rating when listening to a lecture in a math class, recorded on a \(1 \text{ to } 5\) scale where a value of \(1\) indicates low anxiety and \(5\) indicates high anxiety.


item_7
Numerical
Subjective anxiety rating when listening to another student explain a math formula, recorded on a \(1 \text{ to } 5\) scale where a value of \(1\) indicates low anxiety and \(5\) indicates high anxiety.


item_8
Numerical
Subjective anxiety rating when being given a “pop” quiz in a math class, recorded on a \(1 \text{ to } 5\) scale where a value of \(1\) indicates low anxiety and \(5\) indicates high anxiety.


item_9
Numerical
Subjective anxiety rating when starting a new chapter in a math book, recorded on a \(1 \text{ to } 5\) scale where a value of \(1\) indicates low anxiety and \(5\) indicates high anxiety.



Details. This dataset represents baseline psychological profiling measurements collected as part of a major within-study comparison research project conducted by academic researchers in 2022. A sample of \(n = 2,200\) participants was recruited via the Amazon Mechanical Turk crowdsourcing platform. The primary purpose of the original study was to create a high-quality empirical benchmark database to evaluate how well non-experimental causal effect estimation methods replicate the findings of randomized controlled trials within educational training settings. Before participating in any educational intervention exercises, respondents completed the full 9-item Abbreviated Mathematics Anxiety Scale (AMAS) to capture variations in baseline quantitative anxiety. The AMAS is widely implemented in psychometric literature because it efficiently captures two distinct but correlated dimensions of quantitative stress: math evaluation anxiety (items 2, 4, 5, and 8) and math learning anxiety (items 1, 3, 6, 7, and 9).
Source. Hopko, D. R., Mahadevan, R., Bare, R. L., & Hunt, M. K. (2003). The Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale (AMAS): Construction, validity, and reliability. Assessment, 10(2), 178–182. https://doi.org/10.1177/1073191103010002008
Keller, B., Park, S., & Zhang, J. (2022). A new four-arm within-study comparison: Design, implementation, and data. Working paper/dataset documentation.

This dataset represents a random sample of \(n = 1,000\) cases extracted from the massive 2014 national natality public-use file.

Description. This dataset contains physical and academic measurements from a sample of college students, collected to investigate the relationship between backpack weights, student body weights, and the prevalence of self-reported back problems.

Details. Are heavy text books, laptops, and binders physically harming college students? Source. Mintz, J., Mintz, J., Moore, K., & Schuh, K. (2002). Oh, my aching back! A statistical analysis of backpack weights. Stats: The Magazine for Students of Statistics, 32, 17–19.

Details. A group of researchers in Australia conducted a short, three-week dietary intervention using a randomized controlled experimental design. B.14 labor_market_discrimination.csv
Description. This dataset contains a subset of records from a landmark 2004 field experiment investigating racial discrimination in the United States labor market by measuring callback rates for fictitious resumes assigned distinctly African-American or White-sounding names.
File. A comma-separated values (.csv) file containing 4,870 observations (rows) and 7 variables (columns), a selection of the 63 variables in the original data that introductory analyses use most often.
Download labor_market_discrimination.csv (CSV file, 91 KB)

Variables in labor_market_discrimination.csv, with data type and coding key.







Variable Name
Data Type
Description and Coding Keys




education
Categorical
The highest level of education reported on the resume, coded as: \(0 = \text{not reported}\) \(1 = \text{high school diploma}\) \(2 = \text{high school graduate}\) \(3 = \text{some college}\) \(4 = \text{college or more}\)


n_jobs
Numerical
The total number of prior jobs listed on the applicant’s resume.


years_exp
Numerical
The total number of years of professional work experience listed on the resume.


first_name
Categorical
The first name assigned to the fictitious resume (used to manipulate perceived race and gender).

Categorical
Perceived biological sex based on the resume’s first name (\(\text{'f'} = \text{female}\), \(\text{'m'} = \text{male}\)).


race
Categorical
Perceived racial identity based on the resume’s first name (\(\text{'b'} = \text{Black}\), \(\text{'w'} = \text{White}\)).


call
Categorical
Interview callback indicator (\(1 = \text{the applicant received a callback for an interview}\), \(0 = \text{no callback received}\)).



Details. To rigorously study racial bias in employment practices, researchers Marianne Bertrand and Sendhil Mullainathan conducted a massive randomized field experiment in the early 2000s. They responded to help-wanted advertisements in Boston and Chicago newspapers by submitting approximately \(4,800\) fictitious resumes.
The key experimental manipulation involved randomly assigning first names to identical resumes to vary perceived race. Names like “Emily” and “Greg” were used to signify White applicants, while names like “Lakisha” and “Jamal” were used to signify African-American applicants.
The original study’s primary finding revealed that resumes with White-sounding names received 50% more callbacks for interviews than identical resumes with African-American-sounding names.
Source. Bertrand, M., & Mullainathan, S. (2004). Replication data for: Are Emily and Greg more employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A field experiment on labor market discrimination. American Economic Review, 94(4), 991–1013. Harvard Dataverse. https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/JG939E

B.15 maid_mindset.csv
Description. This dataset contains results from a landmark 2007 psychological study exploring the mind-body connection, specifically tracking whether changing an individual’s perception of their daily physical labor could trigger measurable, objective health improvements.
File. A comma-separated values (.csv) file containing 75 observations (rows) and 14 variables (columns).
Download maid_mindset.csv (CSV file, 5 KB)

Variables in maid_mindset.csv, with data type and coding key.







Variable Name
Data Type
Description and Coding Keys




Cond
Categorical
Experimental treatment condition (\(1 = \text{informed group}\), \(0 = \text{uninformed control group}\)).


Age
Numerical
The participant’s age in years.


Wt
Numerical
The participant’s baseline weight at the start of the study, measured in pounds.


Wt2
Numerical
The participant’s weight at the conclusion of the study (4 weeks later), measured in pounds.


BMI
Numerical
The participant’s baseline Body Mass Index at the start of the study.


BMI2
Numerical
The participant’s Body Mass Index at the conclusion of the study (4 weeks later).


Fat
Numerical
The participant’s baseline body fat percentage at the start of the study.


Fat2
Numerical
The participant’s body fat percentage at the conclusion of the study (4 weeks later).


WHR
Numerical
The participant’s baseline waist-to-hip ratio at the start of the study.


WHR2
Numerical
The participant’s waist-to-hip ratio at the conclusion of the study (4 weeks later).


Syst
Numerical
The participant’s baseline systolic blood pressure at the start of the study, measured in mmHg.


Syst2
Numerical
The participant’s systolic blood pressure at the conclusion of the study (4 weeks later), measured in mmHg.


Diast
Numerical
The participant’s baseline diastolic blood pressure at the start of the study, measured in mmHg.


Diast2
Numerical
The participant’s diastolic blood pressure at the conclusion of the study (4 weeks later), measured in mmHg.



Details. In 2007, a Harvard University psychologist conducted an experiment involving 75 female hotel maids. While hotel room attendants experience high levels of physical exertion every day, many do not perceive their labor as actual “exercise.” To test the physiological power of mindset, the researcher randomly split the maids into two experimental conditions.
The informed group (\(n = 41\)) was explicitly told that their daily workplace routines satisfied the U.S. Surgeon General’s recommendations for a healthy, active lifestyle. They were provided with specific examples showing how activities like changing linens, vacuuming, and scrubbing tubs translated into significant physical exercise. The uninformed group (\(n = 34\)) served as a control and received no such information.
Biometric and physiological markers (including weight, body mass index, body fat percentage, waist-to-hip ratio, and blood pressure) were recorded at baseline and again four weeks later. No physical behavior changes (such as diet or outside gym habits) were introduced; the intervention relied entirely on changing the perception of existing behavior. Participants with missing values for weight change have been omitted from this version of the dataset.
Source. Crum, A. J., & Langer, E. J. (2007). Mind-set matters: Exercise and the placebo effect. Psychological Science, 18(2), 165–171. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01867.x

The normalized search interest index for the phrase “sunscreen.” Google scales these values from 0 to 100, where 100 represents the absolute peak search volume during the five-year window, and other values represent a percentage of that peak.



Details. Google Trends isolates a random sample of search traffic to calculate how frequently a specific term is searched relative to the total number of searches conducted during that exact time window. This relative frequency approach prevents raw population growth or shifting internet access rates from artificially inflating the data over time.
Because Google Trends now reports this term at monthly resolution, this file is monthly rather than weekly. It spans October 2021 to October 2026 and is used alongside the weekly gym_membership_searches.csv in the Chapter 12 exercises.
Source. Google LLC. (2026). Google Trends Search Interest for “sunscreen”. Retrieved October 20, 2026, from https://trends.google.com

title: Appendix B — Datasets
text:
B.21 weight_loss_incentive.csv
Description. This dataset contains behavioral and physical measurements from a randomized controlled experiment designed to evaluate whether offering financial rewards significantly boosts weight-loss success and helps maintain weight reduction over time.
File. A comma-separated values (.csv) file containing 38 observations (rows) and 3 variables (columns). Each row tracks the progress of a single study participant.
Download weight_loss_incentive.csv (CSV file, 1 KB)

Variables in weight_loss_incentive.csv, with data type and coding key.







Variable Name
Data Type
Description and Coding Keys




WeightLoss
Numerical
Net weight change measured at the end of the active 4-month treatment period (\(\text{Baseline Weight} - \text{Month 4 Weight}\) in pounds). Positive values indicate weight loss; negative values indicate weight gain.


Group
Categorical
The experimental group assignment for the participant (Control or Incentive).


Month7Loss
Numerical
Net weight change measured at the 7-month mark, which includes a 3-month unmonitored follow-up phase (\(\text{Baseline Weight} - \text{Month 7 Weight}\) in pounds). Positive values indicate weight loss; negative values indicate weight gain.



Details. Obesity management is a major public health focus, but sustaining motivation for lifestyle modification remains a substantial barrier to long-term success. To explore behavioral economics as a tool for clinical compliance, researchers conducted a randomized controlled trial tracking individuals over an extended period. Participants were randomly split into an Incentive group (eligible for cash rewards if they met predetermined weight reduction milestones) and a Control group (enrolled in the same weight-loss program but given no financial compensation).
The trial was divided into two structural phases to test both intervention efficacy and behavioral habituation. The first phase lasted 4 months under active monitoring and intervention. After the Month 4 check, the structural incentives were removed, and participants were left unmonitored for an additional 3 months. At the 7-month mark, researchers conducted a follow-up assessment.
Source. Volpp, K. G., John, L. K., Troxel, A. B., Norton, L., Fassbender, J., & Loewenstein, G. (2008). Financial incentive–based approaches for weight loss. JAMA, 300(22), 2631–2637. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2008.804

title: Appendix B — Datasets
text:
B.22 youth_risk_2007.csv
Description. This dataset isolates demographic and behavioral responses from a sample of American high school students, focusing on the prevalence and risk factors associated with adolescents riding in a vehicle with an intoxicated driver.
File. A comma-separated values (.csv) file containing 13,387 observations (rows) and 6 variables (columns). Each row represents the anonymous survey responses of a single high school student.
Download youth_risk_2007.csv (CSV file, 192 KB)

Variables in youth_risk_2007.csv, with data type and coding key.







Variable Name
Data Type
Description and Coding Keys




ride.alc.driver
Categorical
Riding with a Drunk Driver (RDD) indicator within the past 30 days (\(1 = \text{yes, rode with a driver who had been drinking}\), \(0 = \text{no}\)).


female
Categorical
The respondent’s biological sex (\(1 = \text{female}\), \(0 = \text{male}\)).


grade
Categorical
The respondent’s academic grade standing in high school (9 = 9th grade/Freshman, 10 = 10th grade/Sophomore, 11 = 11th grade/Junior, 12 = 12th grade/Senior).


age4
Categorical
The respondent’s age in years, restricted to adolescent age brackets (14, 15, 16, 17, or 18 years old).


smoke
Categorical
Lifetime tobacco experimentation indicator (\(1 = \text{yes, has tried smoking cigarettes (even a few puffs)}\), \(0 = \text{no}\)).


DriverLicense
Categorical
Whether the respondent has a driver’s license (\(1 = \text{yes}\), \(0 = \text{no}\)); 54 values are missing.



Details. Public safety campaigns frequently focus on the catastrophic dangers of driving under the influence. However, an equally devastating and overlooked vector for youth traffic fatalities is Riding with a Drunk Driver (RDD). To design effective public health interventions and target safety messaging, researchers must identify which adolescent subgroups are most vulnerable to accepting these rides and explore underlying behavioral correlations.
The data in this file is a smaller subset derived from the 2007 Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS), a massive national survey monitored biennially by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The YRBSS focuses on tracking the prevalence of health-risk behaviors that contribute to the leading causes of death, disability, and social complications among youth in the United States.
Source. Brooks-Russell, A., Simons-Morton, B., Haynie, D., Farhat, T., & Litvak, E. (2009). Which young people accept a lift from a drunk or drugged driver? Accident Analysis & Prevention, 41(4), 703–709. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aap.2009.03.004
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. (2007). Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS) Data and Documentation. https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/data/index.html
